newsitem.title: USA: Ford's UAW leaders send rich pact to membership.
newsitem.headline: Ford's UAW leaders send rich pact to membership.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s plant-level United Auto Workers leaders voted unanimously Wednesday to send a new contract deal rich in economic gains and job guarantees to Ford's workers for ratification.

The UAW disclosed that the pact provides the typical Ford worker with $13,910 in new cash compensation over the next three years, and helps them pay college tuition costs to the tune of $1,000 per child per year.
"It's the best agreement we've had since 1976 and we had to strike to get that," said Glenn Maxwell, a bargaining committee member at UAW Local 900 at Ford's truck plant in Wayne, Mich.

The approval by the union's 200-member National Ford Council clears the way for ratification votes by the automaker's 105,000 hourly UAW workers that are expected to be completed by Sept. 29. The tentative agreement was reached on Monday.

According to an outline of the pact distributed on Wednesday, the pact includes an historic commitment from Ford to guarantee employment for 95 percent of its current work force -- a first for the auto industry.

The guarantees are complicated, but require Ford to replace retiring workers at a faster rate if employment at each plant or grouping of plants drops below 95 percent of their staffing levels on the first day of the contract.
The guarantees also provide a mechanism for Ford to temporarily shrink its workforce in the event of a severe market-driven downturn.
But many analysts say that General Motors Corp. can't afford to swallow the job guarantees, because it needs to shrink its workforce by about 50,000 to 60,000 jobs in order to become competitive.
UAW President Stephen Yokich disputed that assessment on Wednesday, but said there was room for differences in the pact between Ford, GM and Chrysler Corp.
"There are a lot of operating issues that are different at each company," he told reporters at the meeting.
He has not decided which automaker to bargain next.

Benefits for Ford include a new precedent that allows the automaker to pay lower wages to workers in new parts businesses and also creates a framework to make Ford's skilled trades operations more flexible and efficient.
Ford may pay workers in the new parts business the prevailing wage and benefits level for that industry segment or for the geographic area in which the business is located.

The new parts provision, however, does not allow Ford to pay lower wages in new businesses that would compete with component work already done by Ford workers and prohibits the automaker from undercutting wages and benefits of non-Ford UAW workers in the same industry or geographic area.
Economic benefits in the deal are generous. It is the first time since 1979 that a UAW contract has contained more than one annual increase in base wages.
UAW members will receive a lump sum payment of $2,000 in the first year of the three-year contract, followed by 3 percent base wage increases in the second and third years of the agreement.

Older workers will find some generous encouragements for them to retire during the new contract. Monthly pension payments for workers who retire before age 62 after 30 years of service will increase by 13 percent to $2,295 after Oct. 1, 1998, from $2,030 now.

Previously retired workers will receive lump-sum payments based on the inflation rate, marking the first time that pensions have been tied the cost of living. Retirees have long lobbied for cost of living adjustments to retirees.

In another first, workers, retirees and families of deceased workers also receive for the first time annual tuition assistance of up to $1,000 for each child or stepchild up to age 25. Retirees also can receive up to $1,000 of continuing education assistance.
Other benefits include an annual Christmas bonus of up to $600 each; a total of 48 paid holidays during the three-year agreement, including a newly negotiated Veterans Day holiday on Nov. 13, 1998.
Existing workers retain their fully paid health care benefits and receive several improvements in coverage, including coverage for prostate cancer tests.
"It's a rich contract," said David Healy, an analyst with Burnham Securities Inc. "I wouldn't be surprised if it increases Ford's hourly employment costs by 6 or 7 percent per year."
